extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social psychology, sociology, history, and general readers interested in crowd behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying descriptive criteria about the characteristics, sentiments, reasoning, imagination, and moral tendencies of crowds as presented in a classical treatise on crowd psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubtfulness of widely observed events
rubrics_metrics.description: The events with regard to which there exists the most doubt are certainly those which have been observed by the greatest number of persons. To say that a fact has been simultaneously verified by thousands of witnesses is to say, as a rule, that the real fact is very different from the accepted account of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass observation often produces divergent or distorted accepted accounts; high numbers of witnesses do not guarantee accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: History as imaginative reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of history must be considered as works of pure imagination. They are fanciful accounts of ill-observed facts, accompanied by explanations the result of reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical narratives often reflect legends and collective imagination rather than precise biographical truth; emphasis should be on how figures are presented by popular legend rather than on 'real lives.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability and transformation of legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Legends -- even although they have been definitely put on record by books -- have in themselves no stability. The imagination of the crowd continually transforms them as the result of the lapse of time and especially in consequence of racial causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect legends and collective representations to change over time and across cultures (examples: transformations of religious figures across regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid remolding of heroes' legends
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not even necessary that heroes should be separated from us by centuries for their legend to be transformed by the imagination of the crowd. The transformation occasionally takes place within a few years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public perception of prominent figures can swing drastically in short periods (example: changing legends about Napoleon over decades).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and exaggeration of crowd sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the feelings exhibited by a crowd be good or bad, they present the double character of being very simple and very exaggerated. An individual in a crowd resembles primitive beings. Inaccessible to fine distinctions, he sees things as a whole, and is blind to their intermediate phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd sentiments tend toward coarse, absolute emotions rather than nuanced positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion and contagion amplify feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Any feeling when once it is exhibited communicating itself very quickly by a process of suggestion and contagion, the evident approbation of which it is the object considerably increases its force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional displays spread rapidly within crowds and intensify due to mutual reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of doubt and tendency to extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplicity and exaggeration of the sentiments of crowds have for result that a throng knows neither doubt nor uncertainty. Like women, it goes at once to extremes. A suspicion transforms itself as soon as announced into incontrovertible evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds convert tentative signals into certainties and polarize quickly; small cues can trigger extreme collective responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of responsibility leading to violence
rubrics_metrics.description: The violence of the feelings of crowds is also increased, especially in heterogeneous crowds, by the absence of all sense of responsibility. The certainty of impunity, a certainty the stronger as the crowd is more numerous, and the notion of a considerable momentary force due to number, make possible in the case of crowds sentiments and acts impossible for the isolated individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity and perceived impunity within large groups lower inhibitions and enable acts individuals would not commit alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empowerment of the foolish and envious
rubrics_metrics.description: In crowds the foolish, ignorant, and envious persons are freed from the sense of their insignificance and powerlessness, and are possessed instead by the notion of brutal and temporary but immense strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd contexts can embolden socially marginalized or insecure individuals, amplifying destructive impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atavistic instincts surfaced by crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: This tendency of crowds towards exaggeration is often brought to bear upon bad sentiments. These sentiments are atavistic residuum of the instincts of the primitive man, which the fear of punishment obliges the isolated and responsible individual to curb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primitive, anti-social impulses suppressed in individuals can resurface collectively when social restraints break down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for heroism and lofty virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Still this does not mean that crowds, skilfully influenced, are not capable of heroism and devotion and of evincing the loftiest virtues; they are even more capable of showing these qualities than the isolated individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds can manifest extraordinary self-sacrifice, devotion, and collective virtue under the right influences (examples: volunteers of 1793, crusaders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective rhetorical methods for moving crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator wishing to move a crowd must make an abusive use of violent affirmations. To exaggerate, to affirm, to resort to repetitions, and never to attempt to prove anything by reasoning are methods of argument well known to speakers at public meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasion of crowds relies on strong, repeated, non-rational appeals rather than logical argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds demand exaggerated virtues in heroes (theatrical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A crowd exacts a like exaggeration in the sentiments of its heroes. Their apparent qualities and virtues must always be amplified. On the stage a crowd demands from the hero of the piece a degree of courage, morality, and virtue that is never to be found in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public portrayals intended for mass audiences should amplify heroic traits to meet crowd expectations (explains theatrical successes and failures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/racial factors shape crowd taste and success
rubrics_metrics.description: A play which provokes the enthusiasm of the crowd in one country has sometimes no success in another, or has only a partial and conventional success, because it does not put in operation influences capable of working on an altered public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messages and cultural products to the specific racial or cultural makeup of the intended crowd; what moves one crowd may not move another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration pertains to sentiment, not intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to exaggeration in crowds is only present in the case of sentiments and not at all in the matter of intelligence. By the mere fact that an individual forms part of a crowd, his intellectual standard is immediately and considerably lowered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect emotional amplification alongside degraded critical thinking when addressing crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance and absolutism of crowd beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are only cognisant of simple and extreme sentiments; the opinions, ideas, and beliefs suggested to them are accepted or rejected as a whole, and considered as absolute truths or as not less absolute errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd-held beliefs tend to be dogmatic and intolerant of contradiction; dialogic engagement is often ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds give authoritative force to inspirations
rubrics_metrics.description: Being in doubt as to what constitutes truth or error, and having, on the other hand, a clear notion of its strength, a crowd is as disposed to give authoritative effect to its inspirations as it is intolerant. An individual may accept contradiction and discussion; a crowd will never do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rejection of dissent in mass contexts; authority and unanimity reinforce conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in intensity by racial/ethnic characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictatorialness and intolerance are common to all categories of crowds, but they are met with in a varying degree of intensity. It is more especially in Latin crowds that authoritativeness and intolerance are found developed in the highest measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that cultural or racial heritage influences the form and intensity of crowd behaviors and dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds prefer force over kindness; venerate strong leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds exhibit a docile respect for force, and are but slightly impressed by kindness... Their sympathies have never been bestowed on easy-going masters, but on tyrants who vigorously oppressed them. The type of hero dear to crowds will always have the semblance of a Caesar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public leadership that projects strength and authority will attract crowd admiration more than gentleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation between anarchy and servitude
rubrics_metrics.description: A crowd is always ready to revolt against a feeble, and to bow down servilely before a strong authority. Should the strength of an authority be intermittent, the crowd... passes alternately from anarchy to servitude, and from servitude to anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate pendulum swings in mass behavior tied to perceived authority strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental conservatism despite violent outbursts
rubrics_metrics.description: Their rebellious and destructive outbursts are always very transitory. Crowds are too much governed by unconscious considerations, and too much subject in consequence to secular hereditary influences not to be extremely conservative. Abandoned to themselves, they soon weary of disorder, and instinctively turn to servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass movements often change superficial details but preserve deep-rooted traditional instincts; revolutionary energy often gives way to restored order or new authoritative structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd 'morality' is transitory and situational
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the word 'morality' to mean constant respect for certain social conventions... it is quite evident that crowds are too impulsive and too mobile to be moral. If, however, we include in the term morality the transitory display of certain qualities such as abnegation, self-sacrifice, disinterestedness, devotion, and the need of equity, we may say, on the contrary, that crowds may exhibit at times a very lofty morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect fleeting displays of high moral behavior (sacrifice, devotion) alongside frequent moral lapses; assess crowd morality in context and by type (transitory vs. constant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts arise from dormant savage instincts and impunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Our savage, destructive instincts are the inheritance left dormant in all of us from the primitive ages. In the life of the isolated individual it would be dangerous for him to gratify these instincts, while his absorption in an irresponsible crowd... gives him entire liberty to follow them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing impunity and reinforcing individual accountability can mitigate crowd criminality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds often act from disinterestedness rather than self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal interest is very rarely a powerful motive force with crowds, while it is almost the exclusive motive of the conduct of the isolated individual. It is assuredly not self-interest that has guided crowds in so many wars... The crowds that go on strike do so far more in obedience to an order than to obtain an increase of the slender salary...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective actions may be driven by obedience to ideas, orders, or sentiments rather than calculated self-gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moralisation effect of the crowd on individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in the case of absolute scoundrels it often happens that the mere fact of their being in a crowd endows them for the moment with very strict principles of morality... The howling, swarming, ragged crowd which invaded the Tuileries during the revolution of 1848 did not lay hands on any of the objects that excited its astonishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd membership can temporarily modify individual behavior toward stricter conformity with crowd norms (including prudishness in assemblies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas accessible to crowds: fundamental vs accidental
rubrics_metrics.description: They may be divided into two classes. In one we shall place accidental and passing ideas created by the influences of the moment... In the other will be classed the fundamental ideas, to which the environment, the laws of heredity and public opinion give a very great stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish transient fashions from deep-seated collective ideas when analyzing crowd thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas must assume simple, absolute, imagelike forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever be the ideas suggested to crowds they can only exercise effective influence on condition that they assume a very absolute, uncompromising, and simple shape. They present themselves then in the guise of images, and are only accessible to the masses under this form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To influence crowds, present ideas as clear, uncompromising, and image-based rather than as complex abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictory ideas can coexist within crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: These imagelike ideas are not connected by any logical bond of analogy or succession, and may take each other's place... This explains how it is that the most contradictory ideas may be seen to be simultaneously current in crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect internal logical consistency in crowd beliefs; contradictory motifs may be active at once depending on cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lofty ideas are debased when popularized
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas being only accessible to crowds after having assumed a very simple shape must often undergo the most thoroughgoing transformations to become popular... It is deprived of almost all that which constituted its elevation and its greatness by the mere fact that it has come within the intellectual range of crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect simplification and loss of nuance when intellectual or philosophical ideas are popularized for mass consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas influence only after entering the unconscious (sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when an idea has undergone the transformations which render it accessible to crowds, it only exerts influence when, by various processes... it has become a sentiment, for which much time is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enduring collective influence requires time and processes that convert ideas into unconscious sentiments rather than immediate rational acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow implantation and eradication of ideas in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: A long time is necessary for ideas to establish themselves in the minds of crowds, but just as long a time is needed for them to be eradicated. For this reason crowds, as far as ideas are concerned, are always several generations behind learned men and philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and communication strategies should account for the generational inertia of collective beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferior, associative reasoning of crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: The arguments they employ and those which are capable of influencing them are, from a logical point of view, of such an inferior kind that it is only by way of analogy that they can be described as reasoning... The characteristics of the reasoning of crowds are the association of dissimilar things possessing a merely apparent connection between each other, and the immediate generalisation of particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical chains of argument are ineffective on crowds; persuasion must use simple associative images and analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds lack critical spirit and discerning judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The powerlessness of crowds to reason aright prevents them displaying any trace of the critical spirit, prevents them, that is, from being capable of discerning truth from error, or of forming a precise judgment on any matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect acceptance of forced or suggested judgments rather than independently reasoned conclusions among crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination of crowds is strong and figurative
rubrics_metrics.description: The figurative imagination of crowds is very powerful, very active and very susceptible of being keenly impressed. Crowds are to some extent in the position of the sleeper whose reason, suspended for the time being, allows the arousing in his mind of images of extreme intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual, symbolic, and marvelous images are particularly effective in shaping crowd perceptions and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds are impressed by the marvellous and visible images
rubrics_metrics.description: It is always the marvellous and legendary side of events that more specially strike crowds. When a civilisation is analysed it is seen that, in reality, it is the marvellous and the legendary that are its true supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To capture mass attention, provide spectacular, legible, imagistic events or narratives rather than statistical or mundane information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre and spectacle have enormous influence
rubrics_metrics.description: For this reason theatrical representations, in which the image is shown in its most clearly visible shape, always have an enormous influence on crowds... The entire audience experiences at the same time the same emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public spectacles and dramatized images can synchronise emotions across crowds and sometimes provoke action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present events as startling clear images; omit genesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever strikes the imagination of crowds presents itself under the shape of a startling and very clear image, freed from all accessory explanation, or merely having as accompaniment a few marvellous or mysterious facts... Things must be laid before the crowd as a whole, and their genesis must never be indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications aimed at influencing crowds should condense complex phenomena into a single clear, striking image and avoid detailed explanations of origins or complex causation (examples: Antony reading Caesar's will).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single vivid events outweigh statistical aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not, then, the facts in themselves that strike the popular imagination, but the way in which they take place and are brought under notice... A hundred petty crimes or petty accidents will not strike the imagination of crowds in the least, whereas a single great crime or a single great accident will profoundly impress them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dramatic single incident will have far greater mass impact than numerous scattered events; visual salience trumps numerical magnitude (examples: influenza statistics vs an Atlantic liner disappearance).
